OK, so issue is that when a normal is almost aligned with the z-axis (with a z-component of 1 but some additional other tiny but nonzero component), but the misalignment is so small that the norm of the vector is 1 to machine precision, then when we go to normalize the vector when it is set in the FourierPlanarCoil, the normalization does not change the z-axis of the normal.
So, that sets the scene for the bug: when the z-axis component of a FourierPlanarCoil's normal is exactly 1.0, but it has nonzero off-z-axis components to it (tiny enough that the norm of the vector is 1.0 to machine precision, thus the normalization of the normal does not reduce the z-axis of it to below 1.0)

Then, we can have this inconsistency occur where we in one part of the compute logic, (the safearccos), the checked quantity (dotprod of normal and Zaxis) is 1.0 to machine precision and thus we trigger the safe route there and return inf
but then inside of rotation_matrix, the norm of the axis (cross product of zaxis and normal) is NOT small enough to trigger the safe route there, and we end up returning things that result in nans (I THINK, I am not sure)

Ok, #2287 will resolve the test issue. I ran [this script](https://github.com/YigitElma/Benchmarks-DESC/blob/master/scripts/02_lcp_prox_jac_freeb.py) with different `jac_chunk_size` values for the objective. The issue in #2239 only happens if `ForceBalance` constraint is chunked. `BoundaryError` is one of the expensive objectives, and we usually need to chunk it to fit to the memory, so I guess this is a good representative case for what this PR can achieve. The above plots show the memory usage for chunk sizes of `[1, 10, 30, 50, 100, 150, None]` and the total batch size is 291. I call the same function 6 times and each time the first shorter peak is constraint evaluation and the second bigger peak is objective evaluation. Note: no chunking could barely fit to my GPU with rematerialization, so the speed comparison is not fair there. The memory usage for very low chunk sizes increases quite a bit, whereas the evaluation is 2 times faster. They converge to the same speed and the same memory as the chunk size decreases. I checked these on my laptop RTX4080 12GB, having similar thing on cluster A100 would help. I think we need to test this a bit more. We usually accept the slowdown for less memory usage.

This is exactly what I'd expect to see, there is essentially a constant memory overhead equal to keeping the residuals in memory. For a chunk size of one this will be noticeable and its proportional controbution will decrease proportional to chunk size. I think it all depends what chunk size you need to run in production. If its typically O(1) then maybe we should gate linearising to skip when chunk size is small (i think even 1-2 will be reasonable). As i said though if you are running with chunk sizes of 1-2 already my gut feel is youd be better off with iterative Krylov solvers in those cases.

Yeah, one weird thing tho (which I realised before but worth mentioning here), sometimes doing the operation in chunks is faster than no chunking or bigger chunks. I guess this depends on the hardware you have and the vectorization capabilities. I mean, sometimes I choose a lower chunk size not for memory purposes but for speed too. I will try to check different types of problems on A100. DESC has many objectives and many options, so it is hard to say whether this is the production run. In the meantime, people are welcome to test it using my repo; it should be quite straightforward when you have a script.

Im surprised that some medium chunk sizes seemed to show a slowdown but I'm guessing this is noise. Also note that for smaller chunk sizes you need more chunks so the speedup might actually be more worth it. I think the interesting thing to check is if you are running at the largest chunk size that fits on an A100 and this PR forces you to shrink that chunk size slightly whether the linearisation speedup compensates for the extra chunks required.

```python
from desc.coils import FourierPlanarCoil
from desc.objectives import ObjectiveFunction, CoilLength
from desc.optimize import Optimizer
import numpy as np
from desc.utils import dot, cross
from desc.utils import safearccos,safenormalize, safenorm
from desc.backend import jnp
zaxis = jnp.array([0,0,1])


def test(normal):
    coil = FourierPlanarCoil(normal=normal,basis="xyz")
    print(f"norm of normal, pre-normalization: [{np.linalg.norm(coil.normal):1.16e}]")
    print(f"coil normal after normalization: [{coil.normal[0]:1.16e},{coil.normal[1]:1.16e},{coil.normal[2]:1.16e}]")

    opt = Optimizer("lsq-exact")

    obj = ObjectiveFunction(CoilLength(coil))
    obj.build(verbose=0)
    g = obj.grad(obj.x(coil))
    return np.any(np.isnan(g)), coil
for comp in np.concatenate([np.array([0.0]), np.logspace(-16,-6,11)]):
    normal = np.array([comp,comp,1.0])
    was_nan, coil = test(normal)
    axis = cross(zaxis, normal)
    norm = safenorm(axis)

    eps = 1e8 * jnp.finfo(axis.dtype).eps
    no_rotation = norm < eps
    print(f"Did Normal of [{comp:1.2e}, {comp:1.2e},1.0] result in nan gradient?  {was_nan}")
    dotprod = dot(zaxis,coil.normal)
    
    print(f"arccos of dotprod: {safearccos(dotprod)}")
    print(f"zaxis x normal = rotation axis: {axis}")
    print(f"norm of rotation axis: {norm}")
    print(f"dot of normal and z axis == 1: {jnp.abs(dotprod) == 1}")
    print(f"is norm of rotation axis < eps?: {no_rotation}")
    print("#"*15)

```

We need a consistency between the two "safeness" logic checks: is the dot of the normal and zaxiz ==1 (or -1), and is the norm of the rotation axis < eps

Because the axis could contain two components which are < sqrt(eps) ~ 1e-8, when we take the norm of axis we square it and they become comparable to zero. 

Gist of it is, we should use sqrt(eps) instead of eps when we try to determine if an axis' norm is zero or not. Making that change results in no NaN.


Outstanding issue: the gradient wrt the normal vector before was ZERO for normal=[eps,eps,1] with eps<1e-15 and then NaN for 1e-15>eps>1e-8. With the change in this PR, the gradient is now just ZERO for normal=[eps,eps,1] with eps<1e-8. This can cause issues in optimization if your coil is initialized as horizontal

```python

# opt problem  fix the geometry of coil, the current, and its center location of the coil

cons = (FixCoilCurrent(coil), FixParameters(coil, {"r_n":True,"center":True}), FixParameters(surf))

opt = Optimizer("lsq-exact")
```

This does not stall out and correctly moves the coil normal so that the dipole moment is parallel to the surface (minimizing Bn)

The test failing is not due to this PR really, as the main issue is that the rotation matrix derivative AD wrt normal vector z component can be really tiny/near zero in certain cases. This leads then to the Hessian scale (~1/diag of hess) being massive. Our epsilon check when Hess size is small (like in the test, only 8x8) allows things like 1/1e-14 to get thru which then completely ruins the scale of the problem. This PR addresses that as well by just slightly increasing the epsilon under which scale_inv is converted to 1 (multiplies by a factor of 10). This was enough to overcome the numerical noise, it seems Using this code: ```python scales=[] scales_inv=[] hess_mats=[] for normal_comp in np.logspace(-16,-1,16): c = FourierPlanarCoil(normal=[normal_comp,1.0,0.0]) angle = np.arccos(np.dot(np.array([0,0,1]), c.normal)) print(f"{angle=:1.2e}") obj = ObjectiveFunction(CoilLength(c)) obj.build(verbose=0) h=obj.hess(obj.x(c)) hess_mats.append(h) scale,scale_inv = compute_hess_scale(h) print(scale) scales.append(scale.copy()) scales_inv.append(scale_inv.copy()) import matplotlib.pyplot as plt plt.figure() plt.scatter(np.logspace(-16,-1,16), np.max(scales,axis=1)) plt.xlabel("off-normal component of normal vector") plt.ylabel("Max xscale from hessian") plt.xscale("log") plt.yscale("log") ``` With the default epsilon we had before in `compute_hess_scale`, the scale was just noise (1/epsilon basically). It was proportional to the normal vector component which made no sense Increasing epsilon by a factor of 10 in this PR at least makes it make sense, this now is proportional to one of the rotmat things which does not really matter anyways as that is always fixed in optimization. There is no more random numerical noise here too

Couple things to note. `CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES` on a local system is not set by default, it is set on slurm clusters because same node has multiple GPUs, and slurm automatically blocks you from using them by setting this. So, I think most of our `set_device` function is redundant since Slurm already gives us 1 device to use (I assume you asked for 1 device). 

I guess in the case where a user requests multiple GPUs (so `CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES` is set and has more than 1 values), where only 1 of them is for DESC and the rest is for some other codes like the issue mentions, we should expect users to handle it without us making any changes. This will not change the behavior for cluster users who only request 1 GPU, but will probably make the life of users who want to use other codes easier.

TLDR; this change works, but I think we can go further and simplify the `set_device("gpu")` part too. The fancy-ish "assign most memory GPU" logic is redundant.
We should still test this on the cluster and see if JAX allocates the memory or not on the GPU.

- removing the `nvidia-ml-py` dependency

- letting users know if they call `set_device` in the wrong place

Only the users that have multiple GPUs visible to the Python process should be affected by this (previously we were picking 1 of them automatically), but I think it is safer for users to decide what they want to do with multiple devices

- requesting GPU 1 can hit an `IndexError`

See #2316, newer versions of jax break some things and we're still working on fixes

Unfortunately, most jax releases introduce breaking changes for DESC. Sometimes these are just small numerical changes that cause CI to fail but in many cases, the changes were to the AD related things which breaks everyones code and makes using older versions of DESC very hard. Because of this and many other problems discussed in #2084 and in our dev meetings, we decided to keep our dependencies tight. We try to be sure that DESC behaves as expected before allowing a new version.

Having said that I know we are late on updating jax version, and I will try to fix it soon. Due to jax-finufft, we cannot allow >0.11.0 jax versions yet. This is another example why we keep the max version, jax-finufft doesn't have a max version cap for jax and it fails with newer versions.

I used Claude for this part, so I want to check my understanding.
jax-finufft accepted extra dimensions. For example, one set of points per flux surface, and it looped over them internally. nufftax only accepts a single flat set of points, with either one Fourier series or a stack of series evaluated at those same points.

The helpers wrap the nufftax call in jnp.vectorize. Its signature tells JAX which dimensions belong to a single transform; JAX maps over any extra leading dimensions, so the old batching behaviour comes back. The signature depends on vec:
- vec=True, (m),(b,n)->(b,m): b series evaluated at the same points
- vec=False, (m),(n)->(m): one series per set of points

Note about the performance regression of newer Jax versions. It looks like the compilation times are the biggest slowdowns. One reason I could find was the new Triton GEMMs (for matmuls), which checks different matmul methods during compile time to decide the fastest one, but this cause very long compilations. Previously, XLA was using cuBLAS kernels, tbh I don't know why they changed this.

When I was testing DESC with f32, I realized that without special care f32 compilations are longer than f64 ones for old JAX versions, and it looks like this Triton transition happened for f32 earlier. This can be prevented by `XLA_FLAGS=--xla_gpu_enable_triton_gemm=false`, which makes the compilation faster (not as fast as before though).

Other comments

Tolerance:
1.  The function approximation done by finufft is superior to that used by nufftax, so nufftax is expected to require tighter tolerance to achieve results of comparable accuracy. Seems like nufftax will only work in double precision then?
2. It is known that jax-finufft gpu is less accurate than finufft cpu.
3. On that point, why does the switch to nufftax require moving from 1e-6 to 1e-8 for stuff like ripple, yet does not also require moving from 1e-8 to 1e-10 for stuff like Gamma_c? In my benchmarking, I needed weakly singular integrands like Gamma to be around 100x tighter than the finite ones to get accurate derivatives.
4. In my experience, doing a comparison of the max difference in the auto diff derivative between nufftax/finufft/matrix multiplies to 4 point stencil finite differencing is more revealing to understand the required tolerance than comparing end result of the optimizer. I think something that would be pretty forward looking in terms of resolving #1998 and supporting other parametrizations of the boundary is that we should implement a class called `ToroidalSurface` for any constant rho surface, that checks to make sure that there are registered compute functions for `Rb_lmn`, `Zb_lmn` . We have to change all of the functions that have `parameterization=["desc.equilibrium.equilibrium.Equilibrium", "desc.geometry.surface.FourierRZToroidalSurface"]` to take `ToroidalSurface` and `Equilibrium` instead.

Then, we can write some logic in proximal that will be able to compute dc/dp where dp are the dofs of whatever toroidal surface that you want to use.

Also @dpanici even though the Fourier transform of the spline surface dofs seems like it should be linear in the spline dofs, this would only be the case if I straight up used the $`\textbf{X}_{i,j}`$ that show up in this formula as the dofs:

$$\textbf{X}(\theta, \varphi)=\sum_{i,j}B_i(\theta)B_j(v(\varphi))\textbf{X}_{i,j}$$

I don't, because I construct the spline dofs in local coordinates about the axis (which is essential to making the splines easily boundable, etc.). To map from my dofs $`\textbf{p}_{i,j}`$ to the spline dofs in the global/lab frame $`\textbf{X}_{i,j}`$ is nonlinear. This means that in proximal we're going to have to compute $`\frac{d\textbf{c}}{d\textbf{p}_{i,j}}`$ every single iteration, whereas we'd only have to compute the matrix once if they were linear.

```python
from desc.objectives.objective_funs import _Objective
from desc.objectives import BoundaryRSelfConsistency, ObjectiveFunction
from desc.optimize._constraint_wrappers import LinearConstraintProjection, ProximalProjection
from desc.examples import get

class Dummy(_Objective):
    def __init__(self, eq):
        super().__init__(things=[eq], name="Dummy")
    def build(self, use_jit=True, verbose=0):
        self._dim_f = len(self.things[0].Rb_lmn)
        super().build(use_jit=use_jit, verbose=verbose)
        
    def compute(self, params, constants=None):
        return  params["Rb_lmn"]
    
class DummyFixed(_Objective):
    def __init__(self, eq):
        super().__init__(things=[eq], name="Dummy")
    def build(self, use_jit=True, verbose=0):
        self._dim_f = len(self.things[0].Rb_lmn)
        obj_bdryR = BoundaryRSelfConsistency(eq=eq)
        obj_bdryR.build()
        self._AR = obj_bdryR._A
        super().build(use_jit=use_jit, verbose=verbose)
        
    def compute(self, params, constants=None):
        return  self._AR @ params["R_lmn"]

eq = get("ESTELL")
constraint = ObjectiveFunction(ForceBalance(eq))

objective = ObjectiveFunction(Dummy(eq))
prox = ProximalProjection(
    objective, constraint, eq, solve_options={"solve_during_proximal_build": False}
)
obj = LinearConstraintProjection(
    prox, ObjectiveFunction((FixCurrent(eq), FixPressure(eq), FixPsi(eq)))
)
obj.build()
x = obj.x(eq)
# this one is full of 0s
J = obj.jac_scaled_error(x).block_until_ready()

objective = ObjectiveFunction(DummyFixed(eq))
prox = ProximalProjection(
    objective, constraint, eq, solve_options={"solve_during_proximal_build": False}
)
obj = LinearConstraintProjection(
    prox, ObjectiveFunction((FixCurrent(eq), FixPressure(eq), FixPsi(eq)))
)
obj.build()
x = obj.x(eq)
# this one has 1s at the diagonal entries
J2 = obj.jac_scaled_error(x).block_until_ready()
```

```
ni = ne.copy() * (1 / Zeff)
```

Thanks, all five taken. Pushed 218ca310d: the patch is now +143 -8 against master (was +258 -11), and the description above is updated to match.

**1. XLA flags.** T4 16 GB, JAX 0.12.0.1, the #1686 script at N = 12, first Jacobian:

| `XLA_PYTHON_CLIENT_` | JAX `bytes_limit` | master | this PR |
|---|---|---|---|
| default | 10.9 GiB | OOM (chunk 3127) | ok, chunk 1410, peak 7.7 GiB |
| `PREALLOCATE=false` | 10.9 GiB | OOM | ok, chunk 1410, 7.7 GiB |
| `MEM_FRACTION=0.5` | 7.3 GiB | OOM | ok, chunk 589, 3.5 GiB |
| `ALLOCATOR=platform` | `memory_stats()` is `None` | ok, chunk 3127, 13.5 GiB | ok, chunk 2330, 11.1 GiB |

Under `platform` JAX reports nothing, so the PR uses master's NVML figure. The chunk is smaller there only through the new coefficient (point 3).

**2. Clusters.** Measured on Slurm (cgroup v2) and in a systemd scope. Slurm puts the limit on the job's cgroup, and the task's own `memory.max` reads `max`, so the parents are read too. cgroup v1 is covered by a unit test only: OpenPBS's cgroup hook (v1) I read in its source. Containers and HTCondor are not checked.

**3. Formula.** Over 26 distinct (N, chunk) points on the T4, N = 10 to 16, the old estimate was exceeded once, by 8% (N = 12, chunk 1500). I raised the coefficient from 2.4e-7 to 3e-7: the worst peak is now 88% of the estimate. It costs time where master still fits: at N = 14, ten iterations take 192 s instead of 163 s (chunk 56 instead of 1213, peak 2.1 GiB instead of 10.2). At N = 11 the time is unchanged.

**4. CPU.** Now one function: the tightest cgroup limit over the process's cgroup and its parents. Reading only its own cgroup misses Slurm's limit (see 2).

**5.** `jax.local_devices()[0]`: done.

I want to make a series of tests at different levels to understand at the ground-level what is happening:

1. A 1D NUFFT vs. direct Fourier evaluation (`nufft_eps=0`) test that samples |B| on field lines before constructing the cubic spline for the turning points
2. A 2D NUFFT test: use turning points from the direct-sum reference to generate identical quadrature locations for both NUFFT backends. Compare the required fields and scalar quantities required later for the bounce integrals, against direct Fourier sums (`nufft_eps=0`)
3. Let each NUFFT backend construct its spline, locate its turning points, and evaluate its integrals. Compare turning-point locations, per-well integrals, and final $\epsilon_{\mathrm{eff}}$ and $\Gamma_c$ values against the `nufft_eps=0` calculation

The direct Fourier sum (`nufft_eps=0`) is:
$F(\rho,\theta_q,\zeta_q)=\mathrm{Re}\left[\sum_{n=-16}^{16}\sum_{m=0}^{16}C_{nm}(\rho)\exp\left(i\left[m\theta_q+nN_{\mathrm{FP}}\zeta_q\right]\right)\right]$
This uses the 33 by 33 grid and DESC’s stored real-Fourier coefficients $C_{nm}$

**Test 1** I have used the W7-X equilibrium at $\rho=0.25,0.50,0.75,1.00$. There are 4 field lines per surface, 20 field-period transits and 64 samples for each field period, so a total of 5,120 points where I have evaluated the NUFFT and the direct Fourier sum. The toroidal angles are uniform so this is a an inverse FFT. But for the poloidal angle, we use a 1D NUFFT. The metric used here is the RMS error || B_NUFFT - B_direct || / || B_direct ||, taking the worst result across the 4 surfaces for different `nufft_eps` error values. Below is the plot result. `nufftax` converts the requested `nufft_eps` tolerance into an integer kernel width using: $`w = \left\lceil -\log_{10}(\mathrm{eps}) + 1 \right\rceil`$ so that's why the error is the same on the plot for two consecutive tolerance. The results are pretty similar and depend on the requested tolerance.

@f0uriest will be bring it within a day

65 Fourier-coil cases on 13 of the example equilibria: 22 `initialize_modular_coils` sets (`r_over_a` 2 and 3), three of them refitted as `FourierXYZCoil`, 5 saddle sets, 6 PF ring sets, the `precise_QA` helical coils, and REGCOIL coils for precise_QA and W7-X fitted as `FourierXYZCoil` at 14 values of N from 2 to 48. Max relative error in B on the plasma boundary with the default grid, against a converged one, by the boundary's distance d to the nearest coil of length L:

| boundary to coil | cases | master | this PR, floor of 32 | floor of 64 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| d >= L/30 | 49 | up to 5.7e-2 | up to 3.3e-6 | up to 2.1e-8 |
| L/60 <= d < L/30 | 10 | up to 0.74 | 4.2e-7 to 3.6e-3 | up to 3.3e-6 |
| d < L/60 | 6 | 0.58 to 37 | 5.2e-3 to 0.34 | 7.2e-6 to 1.8e-2 |

**Separation.** The error falls exponentially in n α for n source points, with α = d / |x'(s)| at the nearest coil point: 2π d / L for a coil parametrised at uniform speed, about half that for the REGCOIL fits. Around a circular coil of radius r, at d = 0.3 r, 0.2 r and 0.1 r, the floor of 32 gives 5.9e-7, 8.5e-5 and 1.6e-2, and a floor of 64 gives round-off, 9.2e-10 and 4.8e-5.

**Coil resolution.** N only adds a second requirement of about 4N to 5N points (measured up to N = 32): at a fixed distance the points needed stay about flat up to N = 10 at d = 0.3 r and up to N = 32 at d = 0.1 r, which is the `max(...)` shape of the floor. Coils that already had 65 points or more (N >= 14 at NFP = 1) are unchanged.

A floor of 64 costs about 1.5 times the floor of 32 per field evaluation on CPU. I kept 32 and put the scaling into `api_fields.rst` (d521c12): say if you would rather have 64.

Not in the table: 4 sets where a coil crosses the plasma, and 4 `SplineXYZCoil` sets, already above 65 points. Spline coils are summed over straight segments, so they converge at second order only.

The last row only swaps the 13 complex exponentials in `rootfun` and `jacfun` for the cos and sin recurrence of `_fourier_series`. `theta` stays within 2.7e-15 of master's in both. At 16,384 points it goes from 0.057 s to 0.007 s. Say if you want that as a separate PR.

<details><summary>The swap, and how it was measured</summary>

```python
def rootfun(t, varepsilon, q_m):
    return t + _fourier_series(q_m.real, -q_m.imag, t)[0] - varepsilon

def jacfun(t, varepsilon, q_m):
    return 1 + _fourier_series(q_m.real, -q_m.imag, t)[1]
```

```python
theta = _map_poloidal_coordinates(iota, alpha, zeta, eq.L_lmn, lmbda)
```

and the third row is its root finding written out with the two functions above.

I also evaluated the geometry factor at candidate magnetic-field minima: $`G=|\nabla\rho|\,\left\|\left.\mathbf{e}_\alpha\right|_{\rho,\phi}\right\|`$. The turning points are determined using the direct-sum reference calculation (`nufft_eps=0`), so those locations are the same for both NUFFT backends. For each surface, field line, pitch angle, we obtain the turning points and compute using NUFFT at the 32 quadrature nodes the fields mentioned just above. Effective ripple uses Gauss–Chebyshev quadrature of the second kind. $\Gamma_c\$ uses Gauss–Legendre quadrature with a sine coordinate transformation. So, the two objectives have different quadrature locations, that's why I have reported the results separately for $`|B|`$ and $B^\zeta $. Here NUFFT is 2D as the quadrature nodes are non-uniform in both $\theta$ and $\zeta$. Hi! Thanks for the comment, but I believe our code is correct. Here you compute the magnetic field from a sheet current _at the sheet current itself_, which is actually the expected value of half_jump here. outside the sheet current yes it is zero, but we are ON the sheet current here so the expected value is the average of the interior and the exterior value, and since the exterior is zero, this means half the jump from interior to exterior. See e.g. https://physics.stackexchange.com/questions/345718/how-to-evaluate-the-lorentz-force-at-a-surface-where-the-field-is-discontinuous

I've been playing around with this and had some thoughts:
- The explanation of J having identically zero columns is wrong, the columns are never zero in any cases I've tried. Bound constraints can lead to identically zero rows, but these don't affect the rank too much. What's really happening is J numerically losing full column rank as you approach a solution (so B becomes singular).
- The cause is the relabelling freedom in theta. The cost of relabelling theta scales like |F| (ie, you move it into a region with higher force error), but this shrinks as you increase resolution and with newton steps, so it hits more as you approach convergence. QR and SVD are generally fine since they ignore these null directions without overly damping others.
- Most of the improvements in this PR are due to the smaller shift for the Cholesky factorization. Iterative refinement (with either B or J) seems to be a modest improvement but not as significant (but its cheap, so might as well keep it).
- `fmintr` sees a similar issue, perhaps even worse because in that case the hessian can be actually indefinite, not just numerically singular, and the shift is again often too large.

I'd propose the following:
- Get rid of the new `trust_region_step_exact_cho_lsq` and put most of its improvements into `_cholmod` + `trust_region_step_exact_cho` - this way it benefits `fmintr` as well. We can keep iterative refinement with B instead of J (seems to do about the same) inside `trust_region_step_exact_cho`, and epdate `_cholmod` to use `delta` as the lower bound and start there. We could then maybe increase by 10x per step until it succeeds, or do the log-bisection between delta and the gershgorin bound
